description: Engineers from Tashkent, colleagues on the same product. Every day we turn raw data into tools people actually use. Over two days we want to do the same for the people who plan space missions.
summary: Earthrise is a web app that shows where a lander at the Moon's south pole would have the Sun for power and the Earth for radio contact. Other tools answer this for one point at a time. Earthrise answers for the whole map at once. On the GPU it traces the terrain horizon in 360 directions from every point, using NASA Goddard's track-adjusted LOLA elevation maps (down to 5 m) and JPL's DE440 ephemeris. Then it runs a whole mission at every point: landing date, length of stay, solar array, battery, Earth clearance, Deep Space Network contact, and the science team's need for permanent shadow nearby. The map shows where the mission works. A landing calendar shows how that changes when the date slips. When a launch slips, a planner sees the new answer for the whole map in seconds.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

You write a mission brief in plain sentences: landing date, length of stay, solar array, mast height, loads, battery, Earth clearance, and whether a Deep Space Network station must see the Moon. One more sentence is the science team's: permanent shadow, where ice can last, within a set distance of the landing point. Engineering wants light and contact, science wants the dark nearby, and the same map answers both. This is the coordination between science and engineering teams that the challenge asks for.

Earthrise colours the south polar map by the answer: where the mission works, sunlight, longest dark, contact, longest silence, battery life, sunlight over 18.6 years and distance to permanent shadow.

A landing calendar under the map shows, for each landing date, how much ground in view meets the brief. With the default lander (450 W array, 3000 Wh battery), a 14-day stay landing on 3 November 2027 works on about 15% of the ground in the default view. The catalogue's connecting-ridge point is about 64% sunlit with 61% contact, but its longest dark stretch, 5 days 2 hours, is over the brief's 72-hour limit. The Malapert Massif and Mons Mouton Plateau region centres fail too: the power runs out. The share rises and falls with the landing date, month by month.

Click any point, or find one of 45 sites (Apollo, robotic landings of several countries, planned CLPS landings, Artemis III regions, three regions from NASA Goddard's 5 m study of the connecting ridge) or type coordinates. You get the lander's-eye panorama with the Sun and Earth against the real horizon, the time to sunset and Earthset, the distance to permanent shadow, and a verdict. One tile answers "If the landing misses": the share of ground within 500 m that still meets the brief. IM-2 came down 250 m from its target. Up to six sites share one timeline of Sun, Earth contact, battery and landing windows. Press play to watch the light move, or use the "Show me" menu: a lunar month of light, a landing date that slips, the view from the ridge, and the best place to land in view, the point with the most workable ground around it. The map zooms in to 1.5 m per pixel.

Five real landings can be replayed: Chandrayaan-3, SLIM, IM-1, IM-2 and Blue Ghost Mission 1. Each says what happened and what the model shows for the Sun and the Earth at that site and date. SLIM came to rest with its cells facing west; the brief can describe a fixed array like that, and the replay uses it.

That covers every objective of the challenge: site choice and comparison, dates, Sun and Earth against the horizon, power and contact metrics, science and engineering needs together, several views, time animation, and plain language.

HOW IT WORKS

A WebGL 2 engine walks the terrain in 360 directions from every pixel of the view and stores the horizon: about 266,000 points in about 7 seconds on a laptop GPU. It nests four grids: a fine focus around the view (5 to 80 m), a 20 or 40 m ring around a 5 or 10 m focus, 160 m and 960 m. The terrain is NASA Goddard's track-adjusted LOLA maps: 5 m from 87 S, 20 m to 80 S, 240 m to 60 S. While time plays, the light comes from the cached horizons, so playback and panning stay smooth. Sun and Earth positions come from SPICE (JPL DE440, MOON_ME frame, light-time and aberration), hourly from 2023 to 2045. A 14-day stay at every point then takes a fraction of a second. An 18.6-year run in 12-hour steps, about 2 s, finds the ground that never sees the Sun and each point's distance to it.

We checked it. Positions agree with JPL Horizons to 0.00003 degrees. Sun elevation at the six Apollo landings matches the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal within 0.02 degrees. The Earth's eclipse of the Sun seen by Blue Ghost in March 2025 is reproduced. We reproduced Table 2 of Barker et al. 2021: seven regions on the connecting ridge, 2,114 pixels at 5 m, two years hourly, at 1 m and 5 m height. All 42 values fall on the right side of the paper's bounds; at 5 m height our average sunlight is 0.2 to 2.2 points above their 1st percentile. On the way we found why the older PDS elevation mosaics are wrong for this: errors along the laser tracks cast false shadows under a grazing Sun, and on the connecting ridge they cut the longest lit period from about 220 days to about 25. So we moved to Goddard's adjusted maps. The GPU engine matches our Python reference model: horizons within 0.02 degrees on average, shares within 0.3 percentage points, in Safari as in Chrome. Against NASA Goddard's 18.6-year visibility maps, correlation is 0.942 for the Sun and 0.976 for the Earth. The app has its own validation page, "How we know it is right", with every check, its sources, and buttons that rerun the GPU checks in the visitor's browser, including a comparison of permanent shadow with Goddard's map. An independent review of the engine code was part of the process, and its findings were fixed.

Limits: the terrain (5 m near the pole, 20 m to 80 S) misses boulders and small craters; no thermal model; the antenna has no pointing limits; the battery model is simple.

WHAT BENEFITS IT HAS

After a slip, a planner sees which sites and dates still work, at once. Geometry decides whether a lander lives. IM-2 Athena landed 250 m from its target in March 2025 and its mission ended a day later; IM-1 and SLIM also lost power or contact to geometry. Students see why the pole is hard, on the real terrain.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A tool a mission team opens when a date moves, and a teacher opens in class. It runs in a browser, with no install and no login.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript, React 19 and Vite for the app, with shadcn/ui on Radix, Tailwind 4, Motion and lucide icons; GLSL on WebGL 2 for the engine; Python with NumPy, SpiceyPy and pytest for the reference model and data build. Hosted on GitHub Pages. The demo video is made with Remotion from screen captures of the app.

USE OF AI

The team chose the challenge, set the direction and made the decisions. Claude, by Anthropic, used through Claude Code, wrote most of the code, tests and documentation under the team's direction, and did the literature and data survey. Every source file written with AI help says so in its first line, and the README states it. The numbers we quote come from tests and comparisons anyone can rerun from the repository. The demo video and the slides are screen captures of the running app, put together by scripts that Claude wrote. We used no AI-generated images, video or audio.

SOURCE CODE

https://github.com/Abulkosim/earthrise (Apache 2.0). Every data source, paper, library, font and sound is listed with its licence in CREDITS.md there.
dataRefs: NASA Goddard PGDA: LOLA 5 m south pole elevation map LDEM_87S_5MPP (the terrain near the pole)
NASA Goddard PGDA: track-adjusted LOLA maps LDEM_80S_20MPP_ADJ and LDEM_60S_240MPP_ADJ (the terrain to 80 S and 60 S)
NASA Goddard PGDA: Site01 region outlines on the connecting ridge (check against Barker et al. 2021)
NASA NAIF SPICE generic kernels: DE440 ephemeris, lunar orientation, leap seconds (Sun and Earth positions)
NASA Goddard average Sun and Earth visibility maps AVGVISIB_85S_060M (used to check our maps)
NASA JPL Horizons API (used to check Sun and Earth positions)
NASA Moon Trek (coordinates of landing sites and Artemis III regions)
NASA Apollo Lunar Surface Journal: Sun elevation at the Apollo landings
NASA PDS Geosciences Node: LOLA polar elevation mosaics (comparison only)
projectRefs: Barker et al. 2021, Improved LOLA elevation maps for south pole landing sites (we reproduce its Table 2)
Mazarico et al. 2011, Illumination conditions of the lunar polar regions using LOLA topography
Glaser et al. 2014, Illumination conditions at the lunar south pole using LOLA elevation models
Bussey et al. 2010, Illumination of the lunar south pole from Kaguya (JAXA) topography: source of one site
IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature (feature names)
LROC, Arizona State University (coordinates of landed missions, including ISRO and JAXA landers)
Claude by Anthropic, through Claude Code (AI tool; see Use of AI in the project details)
Fonts: Archivo and Source Serif 4 (SIL Open Font License), through Fontsource
